back: The application of solid-state electronics to the control and conversion of electric power; its aim is to control the transfer of power from a source to a load.
AC–DC (rectifiers), DC–AC (inverters), DC–DC (choppers), AC–AC (AC voltage controllers, cycloconverters).
$V_{dc} = V_m/\pi$, $V_{rms} = V_m/2$, $PIV = V_m$.
The angle at which the current of an inductive load falls to zero; with an RL load it is beyond π.
$V_{dc} = 2V_m/\pi$, $V_{rms} = V_m/\sqrt2$; D1, D2 conduct in one half cycle, D3, D4 in the other.
Six diodes, each conducting 120°; $V_{dc} = 3\sqrt3V_m/\pi = 1.654V_m$, $PIV = \sqrt3V_m$.
The angle after the natural turn-on point at which the thyristor gate is pulsed; it controls the output voltage.
$V_{av} = \frac{V_m}{2\pi}(1 + \cos\alpha)$.
$V_{av} = \frac{2V_m}{\pi}\cos\alpha = 0.9V\cos\alpha$; $V_{rms} = V$; rectifier for α < 90°, inverter for α > 90°.
Continuous when α < φ = tan⁻¹(ωL/R) (no back EMF); otherwise the current dies at β < π + α.
$FF = V_{rms}/V_{dc}$; $r = \sqrt{FF^2 - 1}$.

front: Ripple factor of the full converter
back: $RF_v = \sqrt{\pi^2/8 - \cos^2\alpha}/\cos\alpha$: 0.483 at α = 0, unbounded as α → 90°.
$V_{dc} = 0.9V\cos\alpha - \frac{2\omega L_{ac}}{\pi}I_{dc}$: the output falls with load current.
Voltage rating about 1.5 × the peak system voltage; also average, rms and surge current, di/dt and dv/dt limits.
An RC network across a switch that limits dv/dt and voltage spikes and improves commutation.
$V_{av} = 2.34V_{ph}\cos\alpha = 1.35V_{LL}\cos\alpha$; each thyristor 120°, fired every 60°.
Ripple-free $I_o$: $I_{L,rms} = \sqrt{2/3}I_o$, $I_1 = \frac{\sqrt6}{\pi}I_o$, $pf = \frac{3}{\pi}\cos\alpha$.
Another name for a DC–DC converter; the DC equivalent of a transformer with a variable turns ratio.
The fraction of the switching period for which the switch is closed.
Continuous conduction: the inductor current never reaches zero. Discontinuous: it is zero for part of each cycle.
$V_c = \delta E$; $L_{min} = (1 - \delta)RT/2$; $\Delta V_o/V_o = (1 - \delta)/8LCf^2$.
$V_c = E/(1 - \delta)$; $L_c = \frac{RT}{2}\delta(1 - \delta)^2$; $\Delta V_o/V_o = \delta/RCf$.
$V_c = \frac{\delta}{1 - \delta}E$, inverted; buck for δ < 0.5, boost for δ > 0.5; $L_c = \frac{RT}{2}(1 - \delta)^2$.
$V_o = -\frac{\delta}{1 - \delta}E$; energy moves through the series capacitor $C_1$ ($V_{C1} = E/(1 - \delta)$); smooth input and output currents.
Four-quadrant: bidirectional voltage and current, so it can also work as an inverter. Buck, boost, buck-boost and Ćuk are unidirectional.
Converts DC power to AC power; single-phase (half or full bridge) or three-phase.
Centre-tapped supply; output ±V/2; $V_{rms} = V/2$, $V_1 = 0.45V$. TR1 and TR2 must never conduct together.
TR1 + TR4 give +V_d, TR2 + TR3 give −V_d; $V_{rms} = V_d$, $V_1 = 0.9V_d$.
Diodes across inverter switches that carry inductive load current after turn-off and return energy to the DC source.
Three-phase VSI; each switch on for 180°, switches fired every 60°; line voltage quasi-square, phase voltage six steps.

front: Why the line voltage has no 3rd harmonic
back: The triplen harmonics of the three pole voltages are in phase and cancel when two are subtracted.
Pulse-width modulation: a reference compared with a triangular carrier sets the switching instants, so the inverter controls its own output voltage.
$M = A_r/A_c$, reference amplitude over carrier amplitude.
One pulse of width δ per half cycle: $V_o = V_d\sqrt{\delta/\pi}$; $V_n \propto \sin(n\delta/2)$.
$P = f_c/2f_o$ pulses per half cycle; $V_o = V_d\sqrt{P\delta/\pi}$.
Each pulse width is proportional to a sine wave at the pulse centre; low-order harmonics are greatly reduced.
Bipolar: both legs switch together, output ±V_d. Unipolar: legs switch independently, output steps to 0, harmonics at twice the carrier frequency.
